name: China distillation and export controls
frame: Chinese labs accused of extracting Western models at industrial scale, and the chip, weight-security and espionage rules being built in response.
question: Do the distillation allegations hold up outside the accusing companies, and do export and espionage controls tighten or loosen? Settled by: a second lab or a government publishing its own counts; a formal US export-control change; or a named company producing records that contradict the figures.

text: As of 14 September the allegation is specific and the rebuttal is political. Anthropic attributes 151 million Claude interactions to Alibaba-linked accounts and names seven China-based AI companies behind distillation campaigns; US agencies named six Chinese firms over industrial-scale distillation in the same week. Moonshot AI, one of the named companies, told TechCrunch it targets $2bn annualised revenue by year-end, double its August run rate, and did not address the allegation in that report.

On the controls side, Dario Amodei tied his pacing plan to blocking China chip sales, a distillation crackdown and model weight security; South Korea's expanded espionage law took effect on 13 September, covering leaks of AI and chip technology to any foreign country; and on 14 September Beijing's foreign and commerce ministries and Global Times rejected Amodei's call to keep curbing China's AI. No named company has produced records contradicting the per-campaign figures.

As of 21 September the controls story has moved from model extraction to hardware and to a proposed government channel. Epoch AI reported that between April 2024 and June 2025 China recorded $3.8 billion of server imports from Malaysia while Malaysia recorded $0.6 billion of exports to China, with unit counts roughly matching at 36,700 declared by Malaysia against 35,500 recorded by China, so the gap sits in declared price: about $17,000 each leaving Malaysia against about $106,000 arriving in China. Epoch estimates the flow "could account for roughly 150,000 H100-equivalents (H100e) of diverted compute" and states plainly that the pattern does not prove diversion. On the domestic-supply side, Huawei said the Ascend 960DT is running ahead of schedule and is expected in 1Q27, three quarters earlier than planned, and CXMT said its fifth-generation DRAM platform has entered mass production at an active-area half-pitch of 11.95 nm with at least 50% more dies per wafer. China's new exit rules took effect on 15 September, allowing travel bans tied to breaches of export-control and technology import-export rules.

The first government-to-government proposal on AI arrived at the end of the week. Talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng ended on 20 September, and Washington proposed a US-China AI dialogue including a notification system for incidents serious enough to raise national security concerns; the US Trade Representative said export controls on advanced AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment were not part of it. Xinhua's readout did not mention the proposal. Separately, a Chinese state-TV-affiliated account accused Anthropic of easing US intelligence access through privacy-policy revisions, and Rep. Ro Khanna called for a Trump-Xi ban on recursive self-improvement. No named Chinese company has produced records contradicting the distillation figures, and no US agency has published its own analysis of the Malaysia trade gap.
states.changed: The arc widened from distillation allegations to measured hardware diversion and a proposed state channel: Epoch AI put a number on a China-Malaysia server trade gap, Huawei and CXMT advanced domestic chip timelines, and Washington offered Beijing an AI incident notification mechanism that explicitly excludes chip export controls.

text: As of 28 September the proposed state channel exists on paper, and the two governments describe it differently. Xi Jinping paid a state visit to Washington in late September. The White House fact sheet says the two countries established the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits, that the next exchange will occur by November 2026, and that they agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for SI incidents; it also records the two leaders agreeing to use the term super intelligence in place of artificial intelligence. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs readout, listing eight deliverables and understandings, describes what reads as the same two mechanisms as the China-U.S. AI Dialogue and a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents, with the next exchange in November 2026. The Chinese readout does not use the words super intelligence anywhere. Neither document names an agency, a threshold or a venue, and UPI reports it remained unclear what kind of incident would trigger the dialogue.

Chips stayed outside the arrangement. The US Trade Representative said export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment were not on the agenda, and Trump said afterwards that the United States is not going to be putting on brakes. Roll Call reported that Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker agreed to fold Senator Tom Cotton's chip location-tracking bill into the managers amendment to the fiscal 2027 defence authorisation, alongside bills from Senators Pete Ricketts and Jim Banks, with House Foreign Affairs Committee counterparts already reported out; none has passed either chamber and Senate Democrats blocked the authorisation over unrelated objections. On the domestic-supply side Alibaba unveiled the Zhenwu V900 accelerator and set a target of more than 20GW of data-centre capacity by 2032. No named Chinese company has produced records contradicting the distillation figures, and no US agency has published its own analysis.
states.changed: The AI dialogue Washington proposed a week earlier was agreed at the state visit and given a date, but the two readouts name it differently and neither publishes a threshold or an agency. Chip export controls were explicitly kept off the summit agenda while three export-control bills were folded into a defence authorisation that remains blocked.

text: As of 5 October the substitution case and the enforcement case were both made in public, and neither was made with numbers that can be checked. Huawei chairman Eric Xu claimed on 30 September that Ascend had exceeded Nvidia in Chinese market share — "It's pretty hard to collect data about the market share of Nvidia in China, but based on the data we have collected, Ascend has surpassed Nvidia" — and said "Even though our chips may be less advanced, at least their supply is assured". Huawei published no sales figure. Xu also said the company does not have enough capacity to satisfy demand in China and has no plans to expand the international market in a fully-fledged way, and two days later a second Huawei executive said advanced-semiconductor capacity in China "is indeed limited", that Ascend chips use that capacity, and that on lithography "right now we're still relying on DUV domestically".

The software layer moved in Huawei's direction the same day. DeepSeek open-sourced six software modules tailored for Ascend chips, mirroring its prior open-source tools for Nvidia's, toward an "independent and controllable" ecosystem. The Register, reporting Xu's claim, wrote that DeepSeek "reportedly released several software tools this week aimed at making Huawei's Ascend accelerators more accessible to other AI labs" — the one sourced link between the hardware claim and the software release.

On the controls, the enforcement record grew and the policy argument sharpened. The Justice Department charged a California man with conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, outbound smuggling and money-laundering conspiracy over more than $300 million of export-controlled servers routed to China through Singapore and Malaysia. A Washington research group, in a study dated September 2026 and reported on 2 October, estimated a stockpile of "over 330 DUVi systems by the first quarter of 2026" for Chinese-owned fabs, with 343 among the modelled figures for cumulative imports rather than operational scanners, and recommended that the United States "ban all DUVi exports to China, including DUVi produced by ASML and Nikon outside of the United States", tying the tools to Huawei in a section headed on the permitted entry of ASML's NXT:1980i despite its enabling production of Ascend AI chips at scale. Reuters, citing the Financial Times, reported Tencent had signed to lease about 100,000 AI chips from Oracle. OpenAI said it disrupted a model-distillation campaign whose core cluster it links to Moonshot AI, identifying related activity across more than 15,000 users. No named Chinese company has produced records contradicting the distillation figures, and no source connected the smuggling prosecution to the lithography estimate or to Huawei's claims.
states.changed: Huawei made its first explicit claim to have passed Nvidia inside China, and DeepSeek shipped the Ascend software to match — while Huawei's own executives described the capacity behind it as limited and still DUV-dependent. On the controls side the week produced an actual prosecution over $300 million of diverted servers and a public estimate of 343 immersion DUV systems in Chinese-owned fabs, with a call for a total ban.

text: As of 12 October the enforcement record has a conviction and the economic case has a number. Reuters reported that Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, a contractor linked to Super Micro Computer, "pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice", entering the plea in US District Court in Manhattan. In March prosecutors charged Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws; Reuters says the scheme began around October 2023 and that the indictment described Sun as "a broker and 'fixer' who facilitated orders and took steps to conceal the scheme". Super Micro referred Reuters to its prior statements that it was not named as a defendant and that the matter had no impact on its business operations. No sentencing date appears in Reuters's account and no Justice Department release was located.

Epoch AI published the first exposure estimate this arc has had to work with. It writes that "In 2022, every $1,000 of Chinese final demand generated $15.2 in revenue for semiconductor producers, 2.7× the $5.7 generated by the same American spending." In its combined shock scenario of a Taiwan disruption plus a China–West trade decoupling, estimating impacts two to three years after the shocks, "Chinese advanced processor prices rise 17-fold and Chinese real gross national expenditure falls by 3%, against a roughly 20% price rise and a 0.6% fall for the US". Epoch says it disaggregated the semiconductor industry out of the OECD's Inter-Country Input-Output tables, and notes the limitation that "our estimates extend only into 2022, where the underlying data ends".

On distillation itself, the detection side moved backwards. A query-only monitoring study reported on 12 October found no deployable detector for distributed model-extraction campaigns at colluder shares of 2.5% or below. No named Chinese company has produced records contradicting the distillation figures, no government or second lab has published its own counts, and no formal US export-control change was published in this period.
states.changed: The enforcement column gained a guilty plea over the $2.5 billion diversion of AI servers to China, and Epoch AI gave the arc its first quantified measure of relative exposure: Chinese final demand generated 2.7× the semiconductor revenue of the same American spending in 2022. On detection the news ran the other way, with a query-only monitoring study finding no deployable detector for extraction campaigns at low colluder shares.

text: As of 19 October the controls are being written on the Chinese side. On 16 October the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology opened consultation on adding 40 technologies to the catalogue of technologies subject to export prohibition or restriction: 23 in artificial intelligence covering large models, agents, compute clusters and information processing, 12 in photovoltaics and 5 in biomedicine. Technologies already in the public domain through open source or published academic papers fall outside the scope of the AI measures. A ministry spokesperson put the split at 14 prohibited and 26 restricted. The comment period runs to 15 November 2026; the catalogue revision is a draft, but a temporary registration requirement for exporters took effect the day the announcement was published and covers exports already begun. Taiwan's economics minister said in the same week that advanced semiconductors and AI servers will be added to Taiwan's export control list, with no effective date given.

The distillation half of the arc gained its first quantified defence and its first named target. Anthropic reported that new defences cut "the amount of data harvested by distillers" by "around 90 to 99%", that extracted reasoning tokens are "consistently 10 to 100 times lower than it was before", and that it has banned "tens of thousands of accounts associated with distillation". It named the accused: "Zhipu, for example, distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3." It added that "The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has since assessed GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date", and conceded that it has not fully met the goal it set in February. Anthropic separately told investors that distillation is 5 to 7 percent of revenue and that the figure will fall.

The market picture moved with it. IDC put Nvidia's share of China's data-centre AI chip market at 34% in the first half of 2026, with shipments down 44% to 678,000 units, and Huawei at 28% on 572,000. OpenCode's maker said a breach tied to a large-scale distillation attack exposed provider API keys for 1.4% of Console users, and its co-founder said attackers probed its systems non-stop for 48 hours afterwards. No US government response to the Chinese draft was reported inside the period.
states.changed: The export half of the arc acquired a text: a Chinese consultation draft naming 23 AI technologies among 40, with a registration requirement already in force and an open-source carve-out, plus Taiwan's stated intention to control AI servers. The distillation half acquired a defender's number and a named defendant — Anthropic says harvested data is down around 90 to 99% and names Zhipu over GLM-5.3 — in the same week a US assessor rated that model the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date.

text: As of 26 October the export half of the arc has moved from consultation drafts to American instruments, and the vocabulary has changed with it. The Office of Foreign Assets Control added five Chinese entities to the Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List on 19 October under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act, blocking their property except for the importation of goods, barring US financial-institution loans above $10,000,000 in any 12-month period, and barring US persons from buying significant amounts of their equity or debt. The State Department's account, relayed through the South China Morning Post, says the targets include a startup founded by a former Google engineer accused of transferring more than 1,000 confidential files related to supercomputing, including Google's Tensor Processing Units. The OFAC notice itself says nothing about what was taken, by whom or when.

The following day the Department of Homeland Security published its order excluding DeepSeek and its affiliated entities from federal civilian agency procurements and requiring removal of DeepSeek products, and of third-party products developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology. The order was originally issued on 24 July and excludes the Department of Defense. Two days after publication, DeepSeek was reported to have raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan; no named source links the raise to the order, and the Chinese outlet carrying the figure does not mention the order at all. Chinese state media reported that DeepSeek and MiniMax had completed export registration under Beijing's new rules and resumed open-source releases, with CCTV framing the measures as establishing regulatory boundaries rather than closing the door on exports.

Treasury's proposed outbound-investment rule, filed on 23 October, renames the sector and widens the prohibition. It records that the change "involves what was defined as AI systems in the Part 850 Regulations and is referred to as 'super intelligence systems' (SI systems) in the Proposed Rule", citing an executive order that requires agencies to use that term in place of artificial intelligence in certain documents, and it would place "development of any SI system" in the prohibited rather than the notifiable category while proposing no technical parameters at all. Comments close on 7 December 2026, so this is not yet a formal export-control change. On the commercial side, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent were reported ordering more than 3 million Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 cards at about $11,400 each, with Nvidia unable to guarantee it can fill the orders and partners possibly receiving only 5% to 10% of the quantities requested.
states.changed: Washington acted on three fronts in five days: sanctions over stolen AI secrets, a published removal order against DeepSeek, and a proposed rule that would prohibit US investment in developing any super intelligence system with no capability threshold attached. DeepSeek raised about $15 billion two days after the removal order, and no source links the two. Beijing's side of the arc moved the other way, with DeepSeek and MiniMax completing export registration and resuming open-source releases.

text: As of 2 November Treasury's proposed rule is published and the threshold-free definition survived into the Federal Register. The notice, published 26 October under RIN 1505-AC94, says the existing Part 850 regulations distinguished among AI systems by training compute and end use but that "no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models", so the Secretary "has determined that it is necessary for national security purposes to define prohibited technology to include the development of any SI system". The definition reaches past models to the scaffolding, covering "a harness for agentic capability or an embodied SI system". The country of concern is the People's Republic of China, including the Hong Kong and Macau Special Administrative Regions, and comments are due by December 7, 2026. It remains a proposal, and the notice does not estimate how many transactions would newly be prohibited.

The capability half of the arc got a government assessment for the first time. Reuters reports that NIST "described GLM-5.3 as the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date" and estimated the model trailed leading US systems by about four months, alongside two private evaluations of the same Z.ai model: Irregular says it "did not refuse any of the tested offensive tasks" and "completed 3 of 13 scenarios end to end at least once", and Epoch AI says it built working one-click Firefox exploits at roughly $1,000 each without triggering refusals from any provider. Reuters reports Z.ai "did not immediately respond to a request for comment".

The distribution question the arc has carried since September now has a customs-based number. Epoch AI's chip-imports explorer estimates 27.4 million H100-equivalents arrived worldwide from 2022 through June 2026, with the United States taking 19.8 million H100e, or 72%, its share rising to 78% in the first half of 2026, and China accounting for 2.6 million H100e, or 10% of compute from 18% of chips by count. Epoch states the limits itself: customs codes mix AI and non-AI chips, the data shows arrival rather than operation, and its China figure ranges from 1.9 to 4.2 million H100e under alternative assumptions. On the espionage side, CNBC reports an Nvidia spokesperson "pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang", and on the Saturday Trump told reporters "We're going to check it out very closely", per AFP, which reports China called the report "groundless speculation".
states.changed: The proposed outbound-investment rule reached the Federal Register with the capability threshold still absent and the prohibited category now reaching an agentic harness, with comments due 7 December. The arc's capability half gained its first government assessment: Reuters reports NIST calling Z.ai's open-weight GLM-5.3 the most capable open-weight cybersecurity model released to date, about four months behind leading US systems, while two private evaluators measured the same model refusing nothing. And the chip-distribution claim moved from estimates to customs data, with Epoch putting the United States at 72% of compute arriving since 2022 and China at 10%. Z.ai has said nothing.

text: As of 9 November the arc's centre of gravity has moved from distillation claims to physical access and to the company that controls it. Nvidia's board statement of November 8, 2026 says it is "initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort", adding that the board "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised" and that Huang "fully supports the review". Three House Republican committee chairs asked Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. No US agency has published a finding, the intelligence memo has not been released, and the board statement makes no allegation about any relationship.

The commercial restrictions tightened in the same week. The Financial Times reported, as relayed here by Seoul Economic Daily, that Nvidia told cloud and data-centre customers worldwide that at least 51% of their services have to be sold to non-Chinese companies, an instruction delivered verbally rather than in writing. Oracle cancelled a chip-leasing contract with Tencent the FT valued at an estimated US$7 billion, covering about 100,000 advanced AI chips across Oracle data centres in Southeast Asia, after US officials raised concerns. Bloomberg reported Chinese buyers expecting about 1% of roughly $70 billion of RTX Pro 5500 orders, with Nvidia expected to supply about 60,000 of the 6 million units ordered at more than $11,000 apiece. Reuters reported about 600,000 H200 chips held in Hong Kong while Beijing withholds approval for large-scale imports. Taiwan's ruling-party bill would jail unauthorised AI-chip exporters to China for up to 10 years, and the US withheld chip-tool licences for SK Hynix's Dalian plant.
states.changed: The arc now runs through Nvidia's own governance. Its board has opened an independent investigation into reporting that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, House committee chairs have asked him for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and no agency has published a finding. On the hardware side the constraints came from both governments at once: Nvidia's own rule that at least 51% of a cloud customer's services go to non-Chinese buyers, Oracle's cancellation of the estimated US$7 billion Tencent lease after US officials raised concerns, about 1% of roughly $70 billion of China's RTX Pro 5500 orders expected to be filled, and Reuters reporting about 600,000 H200s stranded in Hong Kong because Beijing has not approved large-scale imports.

questions.question: Why do the US agencies' list of Chinese labs and Anthropic's list not match?
questions.would_settle: Either party publishing its attribution method, or a reconciled list.

questions.question: What counts as an incident under the bilateral channel, and which agency runs it on each side?
questions.would_settle: A published memorandum of understanding, a named point of contact, or the November exchange taking place with a readout describing the threshold.

questions.question: Can Huawei supply Ascend at the volumes its market-share claim implies?
questions.would_settle: Huawei or a Chinese regulator publishing Ascend shipment volumes, or Nvidia disclosing its China datacentre revenue in a way that allows the comparison.

questions.question: Is China's draft catalogue adopted as published, and does any government respond?
questions.would_settle: Publication of the revised catalogue after the comment period with the prohibition and restriction lists as drafted, or a revised draft dropping the AI model provisions.

questions.question: Does Treasury's proposed prohibition on developing any super intelligence system survive into a final rule without a capability threshold?
questions.would_settle: A final rule retaining the prohibition, or published Treasury guidance defining the covered conduct; or a final rule that adds technical parameters or returns SI development to the notifiable category.

questions.question: Will Z.ai respond to the offensive-capability findings on GLM 5.3, and will anyone reproduce them?
questions.would_settle: A published Z.ai statement or model-card update addressing refusals, a second laboratory reproducing the Firefox patch-gap result, or the NIST assessment published in full.

questions.question: Will any US agency publish a finding on the intelligence memo about Jensen Huang?
questions.would_settle: A declassified memo, a congressional report after the requested closed-door briefing, an enforcement action naming Megaspeed, or the board committee reporting no basis for the allegation.
